name: Moon Rabbit of Korea
description: The Moon Rabbit (daltokki) is the celestial rabbit of Korean folklore, seen in the dark markings of the full Moon pounding rice cakes (tteok) beneath a gyesu cinnamon tree. In the Korean retelling of the Buddhist self-sacrifice tale, a rabbit offered itself as food to a heavenly visitor disguised as a beggar, and the moved visitor preserved its image on the Moon. The legend anchors Chuseok moon-viewing and is shared across East Asia, with the Korean version documented in modern retellings and in National Folk Museum of Korea rabbit-themed exhibits.
appearance: A white rabbit seated within the full Moon before a mortar and pestle, often beneath a gyesu (cinnamon) tree. In folk art it is small, round, and industrious, with long upright ears.
behavior: Pounds rice cakes in its mortar day and night beneath the gyesu tree on the Moon, an endless labor tied to harvest and abundance. In the origin tale it is a selfless animal whose sacrifice wins it a place among the heavens.
cultural_significance: The moon rabbit is Korea's emblem of the full harvest moon at Chuseok, and the diligent, clever rabbit is among the most positive animal figures in Korean folktales.
summary: the celestial rabbit of Korean folklore that pounds rice cakes beneath a cinnamon tree on the Moon
fun_fact: In one Korean retelling the 'smoke' the heavenly emperor set around the rabbit is read as the branches of a gyesu (cinnamon) tree, a symbol of longevity and sturdiest wood.
seo_description: The Moon Rabbit (Daltokki): the celestial rabbit of Korean folklore who pounds rice cakes beneath a cinnamon tree on the Moon.
source: Korean folklore; Buddhist self-sacrifice tale retold in Gwangju News (2017) and Korea Blog; National Folk Museum of Korea rabbit programs; EncyKorea

name: Gwisin
description: Gwisin (귀신) is the Korean term for ghosts and superhuman spirits, rooted in the Chinese characters for 'ghost' (gwi) and 'spirit' (sin); in everyday usage it means the restless dead. A person who dies violently, unjustly, unmarried, drowned, or without proper burial or ancestral rites can remain in the world of the living as a gwisin, bound by han (accumulated grievance). Documented from the Samguk Yusa through Joseon-era yadam collections, gwisin belief sits at the intersection of Korean shamanism, Confucian ancestor rites, and Buddhist afterlife ideas.
appearance: Gwisin are often described as transparent, legless figures that float in mid-air, with long black hair and white hanbok. The cheonyeo-gwisin, the ghost of a woman who died unmarried, is the best-known form and is sometimes faceless.
behavior: A gwisin returns to finish unfinished business or demand justice, and haunting is understood as a plea to the living to acknowledge a wrong or perform a rite. The shamanic gut gives the ghost a voice and leads it out of the world, rather than simply expelling it.
cultural_significance: Gwisin is Korea's central ghost tradition, carried from village wells and magistrate offices into schools, hospitals, and apartments in modern horror (e.g., Whispering Corridors), where it reflects unresolved social injustice.
summary: the restless spirits of the Korean dead, bound by han until the living finish what death left undone
fun_fact: A survey of gwisin by shamanism scholar Tae-gon Kim records 273 individually named gwisin across Korean folklore.
seo_description: Gwisin: the restless spirits of the Korean dead, bound by han and released through shamanic ritual.
source: EncyKorea '귀신' article E0007205; Brill study 'When Ghost (Gwisin) Becomes Demon'; Wikipedia 'Gwisin'; Kim Tae-gon's gwisin research

name: Jangseung
description: Jangseung are Korea's village guardian totem poles, carved from wood or stone and erected at village entrances, roads, and temple boundaries to mark the community's edge and drive away harmful spirits, especially those carrying epidemics. Usually placed in male–female pairs such as Cheonhadaejanggun (Heavenly Great General) and Jihayeojanggun (Earthly Female General), they were worshipped as village tutelary deities and honored at the annual jangseungje rite around the first full moon. Recorded since the Silla and Goryeo periods, most surviving jangseung date to the late Joseon dynasty.
appearance: A tall pillar topped with a carved human head marked by huge bulging eyes, crooked or buck teeth, and an angry grin, sometimes wearing a hat; wooden jangseung are usually cut from pine and stone ones from granite.
behavior: Stands guard at the threshold of the village, scaring away demons, disease, and wandering ghosts so the community stays safe and prosperous. Villagers bow to it, make wishes, and renew it through the communal jangseungje ceremony.
cultural_significance: Jangseung embodied communal identity and boundary protection across Korea for centuries, and surviving poles are preserved in folk museums and revived through festivals such as Cheongyang County's jangseung festival.
summary: wooden or stone village guardian totem poles that ward off evil and mark the boundary of Korean villages
fun_fact: King Jeongjo of Joseon erected jangseung near present-day Sangdo-dong to ward off evil during a royal procession to Suwon, giving the district its name Jangseungbaegi.
seo_description: Jangseung: the wooden and stone guardian totem poles that protected Korean villages and warded off evil spirits.
source: KoreaScience 'The Origin of Jangseung and Ongjung Stone'; KCI studies 'Jangseungje and the Continuity of Community Belief' (Noh, 2025); Wikipedia 'Jangseung'; Korea JoongAng Daily 'Heavenly generals on guard'

name: Samjoko
description: Samjoko (삼족오), the three-legged crow, is the solar bird of Korean mythology and the emblem of the ancient kingdom of Goguryeo (37 BCE–668 CE), later carried into Silla, Goryeo, and Joseon iconography. Believed to live in the sun while a toad dwelled in the moon, it appears as a black three-legged bird inside a solar disc across Goguryeo tomb murals, signifying heavenly mandate and royal authority. Recorded solar-crow imagery reaches the Korean peninsula from the 4th century and is studied in Samguk Sagi-era contexts and archaeological research on sun emblems.
appearance: A large lustrous black crow with three legs, painted inside a red or gold solar circle on Goguryeo tomb ceilings and royal regalia, wings spread as it carries the sun across the sky.
behavior: Dwells within the sun as a symbol of light, kingship, and cosmic balance, serving as a messenger between heaven and earth. Its three legs are read as the triad of heaven, earth, and humanity (cheon-ji-in).
cultural_significance: Samjoko was honored as more powerful than the dragon or bonghwang in ancient Korean thought, and remains a national symbol — it was one of the emblems considered to replace the bonghwang on the Korean state seal in 2008 and appears on Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors FC's crest.
summary: the three-legged solar crow of Korean mythology, emblem of Goguryeo and symbol of royal authority
fun_fact: The three legs of the samjoko are interpreted as heaven, earth, and humanity — a living diagram of cosmic balance in Korean cosmology.
seo_description: Samjoko: the three-legged solar crow of Korean mythology, emblem of Goguryeo and symbol of divine royal authority.
source: Samguk Sagi-era records cited by scholars; KCI study '한국 고대 일상문의 성립 배경' (Kim, sun emblems); Wikipedia 'Three-legged crow'; Goguryeo tomb-mural archaeology (Anak, Ji'an)

name: Ungnyeo
description: Ungnyeo ('Bear Woman') is the bear who became a woman in Korea's foundation myth, recorded at the opening of the Samguk Yusa, the chronicle compiled by the monk Iryeon around 1281. When a tiger and a bear prayed to the heavenly prince Hwanung to be made human, he gave them garlic and mugwort and ordered them to stay out of sunlight for a hundred days; the tiger gave up, but the bear endured and was transformed on the twenty-first day. As a woman she prayed beneath the sacred tan tree for a child, and her union with Hwanung produced Dangun Wanggeom, the legendary founder of Gojoseon.
appearance: Transformed from a bear into a woman after surviving the cave ordeal; the Samguk Yusa gives her no face, height, or features, and 'Ungnyeo' is a descriptive title rather than a personal name.
behavior: Endured eating only garlic and mugwort in a sunless cave while her tiger companion fled, and after becoming human prayed daily beneath the sacred tan tree for a child.
cultural_significance: Ungnyeo forms the earthly mother-line of the Korean origin myth, uniting sky and land, and is read by scholars as a bear-totem figure representing an ancient clan lineage of the Korean people.
summary: the enduring bear of the Dangun myth who became a woman and mothered Korea's legendary founder
fun_fact: The 'garlic' of the myth (san) was likely a native wild bulb such as dallae or mureut, and the mugwort (ssuk) is still a warming staple of Korean traditional medicine.
seo_description: Ungnyeo (Bear Woman): the enduring bear of the Dangun myth who became a woman and mothered Korea's legendary founder.
source: Samguk Yusa (compiled by Iryeon, c. 1281); KOCIS 'Dangun, Father of Korea'; Korea.net; Wikipedia 'Ungnyeo'

name: Korean Tiger (Horangi)
description: The Korean tiger (horangi) is the peninsula's most storied animal, feared as a man-eater yet respected as the mountain god's messenger and a guardian spirit. In the tiger-tale cycle recorded since at least the 13th century, it is intelligent and shape-shifting — a filial, noble 'brother' in one tale and a disguised predator in the next. Wild Siberian tigers once roamed the peninsula, and though extinct there now, the tiger endures as Korea's national animal.
appearance: A large striped tiger, sometimes walking upright in human clothes in folk tales; some traditions read the striped markings across its brow as the character for 'king' (wang).
behavior: In 'The Tiger and the Three Brothers,' it devours the brothers' grandmother, dons her clothes, and springs on the sons as they open the door. Across the wider tale cycle it is a dignified, rational beast that keeps oaths, rewards filial piety, and can be swayed by a clever human's words.
cultural_significance: The tiger appears in Korea's very first folklore — the Dangun foundation myth — and became a symbol of the Korean nation, while children's tales still open with 'when tigers used to smoke' to mean a time long ago.
summary: the feared and respected tiger of Korean folklore, a shape-shifting man-eater and guardian spirit of the mountains
fun_fact: Korean folktales often begin with 'When tigers used to smoke' — the traditional way of saying 'a long, long time ago.'
seo_description: The Korean tiger (horangi): the feared man-eater and respected guardian spirit of Korean folk tales.
source: Korean tiger-tale cycle; Grayson 'Myths and Legends from Korea' (A Tiger Rewards Filial Piety, Tale 124); USC Digital Folklore Archives 'Brother Tiger'; Zong In-Sob 'Folk Tales from Korea'
